site.title: High-resolution Total Alkalinity
site.description: How a quantile-regression ensemble estimates ocean total alkalinity and its uncertainty.
site.footer: Swiss Data Science Center · Numbers are generated from the 1993–2021 run by web/build_data.py · Edit the text in web/content.json

hero.headline: Estimating total alkalinity, and how sure we are about it
hero.lead: A gradient-boosted quantile model learns total alkalinity (TA) from bottle samples. We train **{{run.n_members}} models** that differ in the data they saw and in how they were tuned, then use their disagreement as an uncertainty signal.

sections.title: Bottle alkalinity, matched to satellite and ocean context
sections.lead: The target is total alkalinity measured on water samples. Each sample is paired with the physical and chemical state of the water at that place and time.

items.title: Total alkalinity (TA)
items.body: In µmol/kg, from the **GLODAPv2.2023** bottle compilation. Seawater TA spans roughly 2000–2500 µmol/kg, so errors of ~19 µmol/kg are under 1 %.

items.title: 10 features
items.body: Salinity, temperature, nitrate, phosphate, silicate, bottom depth, satellite sea-surface height (ADT) and the 3 coordinates of the sample on a unit sphere.
One parquet file per year is collocated with gridded products. The run starts in 1993 because satellite altimetry (DUACS) begins then; data back to 1982 exist and are not yet used.

blocks.title: Model inputs
rows: The dominant control on TA; also used as the linear baseline.
Separates water masses that share a salinity.
Biogeochemical tracers; help resolve regional TA–salinity offsets.
Dynamic topography: a proxy for ocean circulation and water-mass structure.
Separates open ocean from shelf and coastal regimes.
Position on a unit sphere, so longitude 179° and −179° are neighbours.

blocks.title: Collocation
blocks.body: Each bottle's time and position are matched to the nearest cell of each gridded product (nearest day, nearest grid point). Day-of-year (sine/cosine) is computed by the pipeline but **not** among the 10 features in this run.

sections.title: From raw bottles to a clean training table
sections.lead: Four filters remove unreliable or incomplete samples. The bars below show how many rows survive each step, computed from the actual data.

items.title: Salinity window
items.body: Keep samples with salinity between **20 and 40**. This drops estuarine and freshwater-influenced water, where the TA–salinity relationship differs.

items.title: Quality control
items.body: Keep bottles with WOCE flag **2** (good) whose cruise-level GLODAP adjustment is at most **6 µmol/kg** in magnitude. Cruises needing larger corrections are discarded.

items.title: Complete cases
items.body: Require TA, salinity, temperature, nitrate and altimetry (SSH) to be present.

items.title: De-duplicate
items.body: Drop repeated records of the same cruise, time, position and depth.

items.title: Feature engineering
items.body: Convert latitude and longitude to three unit-sphere coordinates. These replace raw lat/lon in the model.

sections.title: Cruises are never split across train and test
sections.lead: Neighbouring bottles on one cruise are nearly identical, so a random row-wise split would leak information. The data are cut into **7 blocks of whole cruises**, balanced across salinity.

blocks.body: Blocks come from a stratified, cruise-grouped k-fold (salinity quintiles; fixed seed 42). **Block 0 is the test set for every model** and is never trained on. Pick a split below to see which blocks it uses.

items.title: 5 blocks (~19 400 rows)
items.body: Used to fit the model. Hyperparameters are tuned by **leave-one-block-out** cross-validation inside these 5 blocks.

items.title: 1 block (~3 900 rows)
items.body: Different for each of the 6 splits. Not used for fitting or tuning: kept aside to calibrate the uncertainty estimate.

items.title: Block 0 (3 891 rows)
items.body: Identical for every member. Gives an honest score for each model and for the ensemble.

sections.title: A linear baseline plus a boosted residual
sections.lead: TA is mostly a straight-line function of salinity. The model captures that first, then lets gradient boosting explain what is left.

items.title: 1 · Linear baseline
items.body: Ordinary least squares on salinity alone (polynomial degree 1) gives a first estimate, `TA₀(S)`.

items.title: 2 · Boosted residual
items.body: CatBoost learns the residual `TA − TA₀` from all 10 features using a **multi-quantile loss**, predicting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles together.

items.title: 3 · Prediction
items.body: The final output is `TA₀ + residual quantile`: a median estimate plus a lower and upper bound for every sample.

items: TA_q(x) = a + b·salinity + r_q(x)       for q ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 0.9}
loss = mean over q of pinball_q(TA − TA_q)       (CatBoost MultiQuantile)

blocks.title: Hyperparameters searched by Optuna (TPE, 100 trials per member, 20 random start-up trials)
How the number of trees is set
blocks.body: Each trial trains up to 1000 trees with early stopping (50 rounds) on the held-out inner fold. The final model is refit on all 5 training blocks with the **median** best iteration across folds.

sections.title: 42 models from two sources of variation
sections.lead: Every member is a complete, independently tuned model. They differ in only two ways, which lets us separate two kinds of uncertainty.

items.title: Which data the model saw
items.body: Split k holds block k out for validation and trains on the other five. Members from different splits learn from different subsets of cruises.

items.title: How the model was tuned
items.body: Within a split, seven independent Optuna searches (different seeds) pick hyperparameters from the same data. They differ only through the search path and training randomness.

blocks.title: All members
blocks.hint: Each cell is one model: rows are splits, columns are HPO replicates. Click a cell for its tuned hyperparameters and test scores.

blocks.body: The ensemble prediction is the **mean** of the members' quantiles. Because all members share the same test block, every difference between them on that block comes from the two axes above.

sections.title: Disagreement between members is a measure of doubt
sections.lead: Two signals are available for every prediction: the spread of the member medians, and the width of the predicted quantile band. Explore how they behave on real held-out samples.

items.title: Member spread
items.body: Standard deviation of the 42 member medians. It grows where models disagree, typically in sparsely sampled regions.

items.title: Quantile width
items.body: Predicted Q90 − Q10 divided by 2.563, which equals one standard deviation for a normal distribution.

items.title: Split vs. HPO
items.body: By the law of total variance, member variance = variance between splits + average variance within a split (between HPO replicates).

blocks.title: Where does the member variance come from?

blocks.body: On the held-out test block the spread of member medians correlates with the absolute error at **r = {{spread_vs_error.corr_abs_err.member_std|2}}**, versus **r = {{spread_vs_error.corr_abs_err.scaled_iqr|2}}** for the scaled quantile width.

blocks.title: Does the uncertainty predict the error?
Read this as a ranking, not an error bar
blocks.body: Higher member spread goes with larger errors (the curves rise), but the raw spread is several times smaller than the actual RMSE in every bin. It tells you **which predictions to trust less**, not yet **by how many µmol/kg**. Rescaling on the validation blocks is the planned next step.

sections.title: What is still open
sections.lead: This page describes the current state of the work, not a finished product.

blocks.title: Intervals are too narrow
blocks.body: The nominal 80 % interval (Q10–Q90) covers **{{ensemble_scores.all.interval_80pct_coverage|pct}}** of held-out test samples. Averaging members does not fix this, so the bands should be widened or rescaled.

items.title: Calibrate on validation blocks
items.body: Use validation RMSE to choose between the member std and the scaled Q90 − Q10 as the uncertainty estimate, then rescale it. Compare against the untouched test block.

items.title: Extend the record
items.body: Data from 1982–1992 exist but are excluded because altimetry is missing. Dropping SSH or filling it would extend the training period.

items.title: Independent check
items.body: Compare predictions with the BATS and HOT time series, which were not used for tuning.

items.title: Full-period inference
items.body: Apply the ensemble to the gridded 8-day, 0.25° fields, where the inputs are gridded products rather than bottle measurements.
